claims.text: Local chemical ordering governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local chemical ordering creates regions with different cohesive energies.
Regions with different cohesive energies initiate phase changes at different temperatures.
The initial nanoparticles are solid and chemically homogeneous.
The nanoparticles have a nominally equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu composition.
Local compositional fluctuations and clustering of particular elements produce heterogeneous bonding strengths within each nanoparticle.
Pockets with different cohesive energies act as initiation sites for melting.
Multiple melting-initiation sites cause a broadened and temporally heterogeneous transition rather than a sharp, uniform melting point.
Relative to single-metal nanoparticles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit multiple spatially localized melting events.
Relative to single-metal nanoparticles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will melt over a broader temperature range.
Au or Pd single-metal nanoparticles typically undergo a sharp and uniform melting transition.
Surface and finite-size effects are prominent for nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in size.
The proposed mechanism applies to approximately 5–50 nm particles subjected to rapid heating, while its applicability to larger particles or near-equilibrium conditions is uncertain.
Direct studies of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are sparse, so the relative contributions of chemical ordering, surface reconstruction, and strain remain uncertain.

The hypothesis would be falsified if the alloy nanoparticles show a sharp, uniform transition indistinguishable from the single-metal control and show no spatial correlation between chemical ordering and melting behavior.

contradictions.description: The initial particles are described as chemically homogeneous, but the proposed mediator requires local compositional fluctuations and clustering. This could be reconciled if 'homogeneous' means only macroscopically or nominally homogeneous, but that distinction is not stated.
